note.title: Converging and diverging lenses; measuring focal length
note.subject: science

mustKnow: A converging (convex) lens is fat in the middle and brings parallel rays to the principal focus
A diverging (concave) lens is thin in the middle and spreads parallel rays apart
The focal length is the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus
The distant-object method: distant object, screen moved until sharp, lens-to-screen distance measured
A mean leaves out any anomalous reading

notOnThisSpec: Magnification as a calculation (image height divided by object height)
The power of a lens in dioptres
The eye, long sight and short sight and their correction

mustBeAbleTo: Name a lens as converging or diverging from its shape and from its ray-diagram symbol
Describe what each kind of lens does to rays arriving parallel to the principal axis
Label the principal axis, the optical centre, the principal focus and the focal length
For a converging lens, define the focal length by naming the two points it runs between
Say where the principal focus of a diverging lens is and how it is found
Describe the distant-object method and name the apparatus it uses
Explain why the object has to be distant, in terms of parallel rays
Spot an anomalous reading and take a mean without it
Say that a real image can be caught on a screen, and why
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Lenses open with a picture and a one-mark naming question, then the definition of focal length, then the three-item method. Summer 2025 Foundation Q3(a) gave three marks for that method. Unit 7 Physics Booklet B has set the focal-length definition, the screen needed for a real image, and a mean with an anomalous reading in it.
traps: Swapping converging and diverging, or convex and concave (Summer 2024 P2 F Q2)
Not knowing where to label the principal focus on a lens diagram (Summer 2025 P2 H Q7)
Leaving the scientific terms out of the focal-length definition, when the scheme gives a mark each for distance, focus and centre (Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2)
Giving only one of the three items of the distant-object method: a distant object, a screen moved until sharp, and the lens-to-screen distance (Summer 2025 P2 F Q3)
Not realising that a screen is needed to see the real image the lens forms (Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2; Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q4)
Averaging an anomalous reading in with the ones that agree (Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2; Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q4)
Recognising a concave lens, as most did, but not knowing the rules for the rays that follow (Summer 2023 P2 F Q8)

noteBlocks.lede: A lens is a piece of glass with curved faces, and every ray that crosses it is refracted twice. One shape brings light together; the other spreads it apart. Which one you have, and how strongly it bends light, is the whole of this topic.
can: Tell a converging lens from a diverging one, by shape and by symbol
Define focal length using the principal focus and the centre of the lens
Measure a focal length with a distant object, a screen and a metre rule

noteBlocks.md: A **converging** lens (also called convex) is **fat in the middle** and brings light together. A **diverging** lens (concave) is **thin in the middle** and spreads light apart. In a ray diagram you never draw the curved glass: you draw a vertical line with arrowheads, pointing **outwards** for converging and **inwards** for diverging.

noteBlocks.stem: A ray diagram shows a lens drawn as a vertical line whose arrowheads point inwards. Name the lens, and describe the shape of its glass. [2]

steps.working: Inward arrowheads: the symbol for a diverging lens, also called concave.
steps.decision: Read the symbol first: inwards means diverging, outwards converging.

steps.working: So its glass is thinner in the middle than at its edges.
steps.decision: The shape and the name go together; say both.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two lenses lie on a bench, one fat in the middle and one thin in the middle. Which one brings light together?
options: the one that is fat in the middle
the one that is thin in the middle
neither: they both converge light
noteBlocks.answer: the one that is fat in the middle
noteBlocks.explain: The one that is fat in the middle: a converging, or convex, lens. Thin in the middle spreads light apart. Say the shape and the name together every time, so the two never swap.

optionNotes.option: the one that is thin in the middle
optionNotes.why: Thin in the middle is the diverging (concave) lens: it spreads parallel light apart.

optionNotes.option: neither: they both converge light
optionNotes.why: Only the lens that is fat in the middle converges light; the thin one spreads it apart.

twin.prompt: A ray diagram shows a lens as a vertical line with its arrowheads pointing outwards. Which lens is it?
options: a converging lens
a diverging lens
it could be either
twin.explain: Outward arrowheads are the symbol for a converging lens; inward ones mean diverging.

optionNotes.option: a diverging lens
optionNotes.why: The diverging symbol has its arrowheads pointing inwards; outwards means converging.

optionNotes.option: it could be either
optionNotes.why: The arrowheads settle it: outwards is always converging, inwards always diverging.

noteBlocks.text: 2. A converging lens and its focus

noteBlocks.md: Rays that arrive **parallel to the principal axis** are refracted at both faces, and a converging lens brings them all to **one point** on the axis. That point is the **principal focus**, **F**. A lens has an F on each side, the same distance out.

noteBlocks.title: Why parallel rays, and not any old rays?
noteBlocks.md: Because only parallel rays all meet at the same point. Rays from a nearby object arrive spread out and meet somewhere else, further from the lens — which is why the focal length is defined for parallel rays, and why the practical uses a distant object.

noteBlocks.stem: A magnifying glass held in sunlight makes a small bright dot on paper 12 cm below it. Explain what is happening, and state the lens's focal length. [3]

steps.working: Sunlight comes from so far away that its rays arrive parallel.
steps.decision: Start from the light arriving: parallel rays are the ones a lens brings to one point.

steps.working: The lens refracts them so that they all meet at one point: the bright dot is F.
steps.decision: Every ray passes through the same point, so the light's energy is concentrated there.

steps.working: The dot is 12 cm from the lens, so the focal length is 12 cm.
steps.decision: The focal length runs from the lens to F.

noteBlocks.prompt: Rays arriving parallel to the principal axis of a converging lens all pass through one point on the axis. What is that point called? (two words)
noteBlocks.answer: principal focus | the principal focus | principal focal point | focal point | the focal point
noteBlocks.explain: The principal focus, or focal point, marked F on every diagram, one on each side of the lens. Summer 2025 Higher examiners found many unsure where F should be marked.

twin.prompt: What is the distance from the centre of a converging lens to its principal focus called? (two words)
twin.explain: The focal length: the distance from the optical centre of the lens to F.

noteBlocks.md: A **diverging** lens spreads parallel rays apart, so they never meet. Trace them **backwards** as dashed lines and they seem to come from one point on the **same side as the light came from**: its principal focus. CCEA asks you to name the two lenses and say what each does; ray diagrams for diverging lenses are not on this specification.

noteBlocks.stem: A student's diagram shows rays leaving a lens spreading apart, as if from a point 9 cm in front of the lens. Name the lens, and state its focal length. [2]

steps.working: Spreading apart: a diverging lens.
steps.decision: Only a diverging lens spreads parallel rays; a converging one brings them together.

steps.working: They seem to come from a point 9 cm in front of it: that point is F, so the focal length is 9 cm.
steps.decision: For a diverging lens F is on the side the light comes from, found by tracing back.

noteBlocks.prompt: Light from a distant street lamp passes through a lens that is thinner at its centre than at its edges. What happens to the rays after the lens?
options: they spread apart, as though coming from a point on the near side
they meet at a point on the far side
they carry straight on without bending
noteBlocks.answer: they spread apart, as though coming from a point on the near side
noteBlocks.explain: It is a diverging lens, so the rays spread apart. Traced back, they seem to come from a point on the near side, the side the light came from. Meeting at a point on the far side is what a converging lens does.

optionNotes.option: they meet at a point on the far side
optionNotes.why: Meeting on the far side is the converging lens; a lens thin in the middle spreads the rays apart.

optionNotes.option: they carry straight on without bending
optionNotes.why: Both kinds of lens bend the rays; only a ray through the optical centre goes straight on.

twin.prompt: Where is the principal focus of a diverging lens?
options: on the same side as the light comes from
on the far side, where the rays meet
at the centre of the lens
twin.answer: on the same side as the light comes from
twin.explain: The rays spread after the lens, so its F is found by tracing them back: it is on the side the light comes from.

optionNotes.option: on the far side, where the rays meet
optionNotes.why: The rays from a diverging lens never meet on the far side; they spread apart.

optionNotes.option: at the centre of the lens
optionNotes.why: F is one focal length from the centre, on the side the light comes from, where the traced-back lines meet.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these does CCEA Double Award Science ask you to do with a diverging lens?
options: recognise it and say that it spreads parallel rays apart
draw a full ray diagram to find the image it forms
calculate the magnification of the image it forms
noteBlocks.answer: recognise it and say that it spreads parallel rays apart
noteBlocks.explain: Recognise it, and say what it does to parallel rays. Ray diagrams for diverging lenses and the magnification calculation belong to the separate-Physics courses.

optionNotes.option: draw a full ray diagram to find the image it forms
optionNotes.why: Diverging-lens ray diagrams are separate-Physics content; CCEA Double Award asks you only to recognise the lens and say what it does.

optionNotes.option: calculate the magnification of the image it forms
optionNotes.why: Magnification as a calculation is not on this specification for any lens.

twin.prompt: Which of these must you be able to do with a converging lens on this course?
options: define its focal length and measure it with a distant object
work out its focal length from the lens equation
calculate the magnification of its image as a number
twin.answer: define its focal length and measure it with a distant object
twin.explain: The specification asks you to define a converging lens's focal length and measure it with a distant object; the lens equation and magnification are not on it.

optionNotes.option: work out its focal length from the lens equation
optionNotes.why: The lens equation belongs to other courses; here the focal length is defined and measured.

optionNotes.option: calculate the magnification of its image as a number
optionNotes.why: Magnification as a number is not asked for; images are described in words.

noteBlocks.md: The **principal axis** is the line through the middle of the lens, at right angles to it. The **optical centre** is where the axis crosses the lens. F is marked on **both** sides, the same distance out. The **focal length** is the distance from the **optical centre** to the **principal focus**: write the word distance and name both points, every time.

noteBlocks.stem: On a lens diagram, point O is where the principal axis crosses a converging lens, and F is marked 7 cm from O on the right. Where does the other F go, and what is the focal length? [2]

steps.working: The other F goes 7 cm from O on the left.
steps.decision: A lens has an F on each side, the same distance out.

steps.working: The focal length is the distance from O to F: 7 cm.
steps.decision: O is the point every lens distance is measured from.

noteBlocks.prompt: Complete the definition. A converging lens's focal length is the distance from the principal focus to the __ of the lens. (two words)
noteBlocks.answer: optical centre | centre | the optical centre
noteBlocks.explain: The optical centre, the point O where the axis crosses the lens. Summer 2024 Booklet B gave a mark each for distance, focus and centre, and fewer candidates recalled the scientific term.

twin.prompt: Complete the definition: the focal length is the __ from the optical centre to the principal focus. (one word)
twin.explain: Distance: the definition names what is measured, a distance, and the two points it runs between.

noteBlocks.md: Point the lens at something **far away**, such as a window across the room, and hold a **screen** behind it. Move the screen until the image on it is **sharp**, then measure the distance between the lens's centre and the screen with a **metre rule**. Light from a distant object arrives almost parallel, so the sharp image forms at F, and that distance is the focal length.

noteBlocks.caption: Distant object, sharp image, lens to screen: the focal length.

noteBlocks.stem: A student has a converging lens, a white screen, a metre rule and a window at the far end of the lab. Describe how she finds the focal length. [3]

steps.working: Point the lens at the distant window.
steps.decision: Its light arrives almost parallel, which is what makes the image form at F.

steps.working: Move the screen behind the lens until the window's image on it is sharp.
steps.decision: Only at the sharp position is the screen at F; a blurred image means it is too near or too far.

steps.working: Measure the distance between the lens's centre and the screen with the metre rule.
steps.decision: That distance is the focal length; repeat it and take a mean.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why must the screen be moved until the image is sharp before the distance is measured?
options: only when the image is sharp is the screen at F
a sharp image is brighter and easier to measure
the screen has to touch the lens first
noteBlocks.answer: only when the image is sharp is the screen at F
noteBlocks.explain: The parallel light meets at F, and the image is sharp only where the rays meet. At any other place the screen shows a blur, and the distance measured is not the focal length.

optionNotes.option: a sharp image is brighter and easier to measure
optionNotes.why: Brightness is not the reason: a sharp image marks the point where the rays meet, which is F.

optionNotes.option: the screen has to touch the lens first
optionNotes.why: The screen starts wherever you like; what matters is stopping where the image is sharp, at F.

twin.prompt: Why must the object be a long way from the lens in this method?
options: so that its light arrives almost parallel
so that its image is brighter
so that its image is larger
twin.answer: so that its light arrives almost parallel
twin.explain: Parallel rays are the ones a converging lens brings to F, so only a distant object's image forms at F.

optionNotes.option: so that its image is brighter
optionNotes.why: A distant object gives a dimmer image, if anything; the point is that its light arrives almost parallel.

optionNotes.option: so that its image is larger
optionNotes.why: A distant object gives a small image; distance matters because its light arrives almost parallel.

noteBlocks.md: Measure the distance **three or four times**. If one reading is far from the others it is **anomalous**: something went wrong that time. Leave it out, add the readings that agree, and divide by **how many you used**.

noteBlocks.stem: Four lens-to-screen readings are 21.3 cm, 20.9 cm, 25.6 cm and 21.1 cm. Find the focal length, to one decimal place. [2]

steps.working: 25.6 cm is far from the other three: it is anomalous, so leave it out.
steps.decision: Spot the odd one out before any arithmetic.
Divide by the three readings used, not the four taken.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student's lens-to-screen readings are 9.4 cm, 9.6 cm, 9.5 cm and 13.1 cm. Ignoring the anomalous reading, what is the focal length in cm, to one decimal place?
noteBlocks.explain: 13.1 cm is the anomaly, so leave it out: (9.4 + 9.6 + 9.5) ÷ 3 = 28.5 ÷ 3 = 9.5 cm. Summer 2024 Booklet B examiners saw an anomaly averaged in, which cost both marks.

twin.prompt: Readings of 12.2 cm, 16.9 cm, 12.4 cm and 12.3 cm are taken. Leaving out the anomaly, what is the focal length in cm, to one decimal place?

noteBlocks.md: A converging lens that is **fatter in the middle** bends each ray through a bigger angle, so parallel rays meet **closer** to the lens: its focal length is **shorter**. A thinner converging lens bends light less, and its focal length is longer.

noteBlocks.stem: A student swaps her lens for a thinner converging lens made of the same glass. Predict where the sharp image of the window now forms, and explain. [2]

steps.working: A thinner lens bends each ray through a smaller angle.
steps.decision: Start from what the shape does to each ray.

steps.working: So the rays meet further from the lens: she moves the screen back, and the focal length is longer.
steps.decision: Less bending means a longer distance before the rays meet.

noteBlocks.task: Drag the focal-length slider from its smallest value to its largest and watch the two F marks move. Notice which setting makes the lens fattest, and check the pattern in the See it.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student makes a converging lens fatter in the middle, in the simulation. What happens to its focal length?
options: it gets shorter
it gets longer
it does not change
noteBlocks.explain: Shorter. A fatter lens bends each ray through a bigger angle, so parallel rays meet closer to the lens.

optionNotes.option: it gets longer
optionNotes.why: Longer goes with a thinner lens, which bends light less; a fatter lens bends it more, so the rays meet sooner.

optionNotes.option: it does not change
optionNotes.why: The shape sets how much each ray bends, so a fatter lens brings the rays together closer to it.

twin.prompt: Which bends light more: a converging lens with a focal length of 6 cm or one with 25 cm?
options: the 6 cm lens
the 25 cm lens
both bend light equally
twin.explain: The 6 cm lens brings parallel rays together sooner, so it bends each ray more; it is also the fatter lens.

optionNotes.option: the 25 cm lens
optionNotes.why: A longer focal length means the rays take further to meet, so each has been bent less.

optionNotes.option: both bend light equally
optionNotes.why: Different focal lengths mean different bending: the shorter one bends light more.

noteBlocks.md: **Name it from a picture.** The paper shows a lens or its symbol and gives a mark for naming it (Summer 2024 Foundation). **Complete the definition.** A sentence with gaps for distance, focus and centre (Summer 2024 Booklet B, Summer 2026 Foundation). **Pick the apparatus.** Choose the three things the method needs from a longer list (Summer 2025 Foundation).

noteBlocks.stem: From this list, choose the three things needed to find a focal length by the distant-object method: stopwatch, screen, thermometer, metre rule, a window across the room, a lamp beside the lens. [3]

steps.working: A window across the room: a distant object.
steps.decision: Its light arrives almost parallel; a lamp beside the lens is far too near to count as distant.

steps.working: A screen, to catch the sharp image.
steps.decision: The image is real, so a screen can show it.

steps.working: A metre rule, for the lens-to-screen distance.
steps.decision: Nothing is timed or heated, so the other two are not needed.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the distant-object method, which of these is done last?
options: measure from the lens to the screen
point the lens at the distant object
move the screen until the image is sharp
noteBlocks.answer: measure from the lens to the screen
noteBlocks.explain: Aim at the distant object, move the screen until the image is sharp, and only then measure: the distance means nothing until the screen is at F.

optionNotes.option: point the lens at the distant object
optionNotes.why: Pointing at the distant object comes first: without it there is no image to sharpen.

optionNotes.option: move the screen until the image is sharp
optionNotes.why: Sharpening comes before measuring: the screen has to reach F before the distance is the focal length.

twin.prompt: In the distant-object method, which of these is done first?
options: point the lens at the distant object
measure from the lens to the screen
move the screen until the image is sharp
twin.answer: point the lens at the distant object
twin.explain: The distant object comes first: its parallel light is what the lens brings to F.

optionNotes.option: measure from the lens to the screen
optionNotes.why: Measuring is the last step, once the image on the screen is sharp.

optionNotes.option: move the screen until the image is sharp
optionNotes.why: There is nothing to sharpen until the lens is pointed at the distant object.

noteBlocks.md:
Name a lens as converging or diverging from its shape or its symbol.
Say what each lens does to rays arriving parallel to the axis.
Define the focal length: the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.
Measure it with a distant object, a screen and a metre rule, leaving any anomaly out of the mean.

Expect a lens or its symbol to name, the definition of focal length with its three key words, and three marks for the method: a distant object, a screen moved until the image is sharp, and the lens-to-screen distance. If readings disagree, leave the odd one out of the mean.

workedExamples.stem: A lens is thin in the middle and thick at its edges. Name it, say what it does to parallel rays, and state where its principal focus lies.

steps.working: Thin in the middle, thick at the edges: this is a diverging lens, also called concave.
steps.decision: Naming it first fixes everything else, and swapping the two names is the commonest slip on this topic.

options: because a lens thin in the middle spreads light out
because a lens thin in the middle brings light together
because the name depends on the glass, not the shape
whyMenu.explain: The shape decides it. Fat in the middle converges; thin in the middle diverges.

steps.working: Rays arriving parallel to the principal axis are spread apart as they pass through.
steps.decision: They never cross, so there is no point on the far side where they all meet.

steps.working: Trace the spreading rays backwards with dashed lines. Those lines cross at one point.
steps.decision: That point is the principal focus, and it lies on the same side as the light came from.

accepted: On the same side as the light came from, where the backward extensions cross.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: It is a diverging (concave) lens. It spreads parallel rays apart, and its principal focus is the point on the near side where the backward extensions of those rays cross.

twin.stem: A lens is fat in the middle. Name the kind of lens it is.

workedExamples.stem: A student measures the lens-to-screen distance four times and records 32.4 cm, 31.8 cm, 27.5 cm and 32.1 cm. Find the focal length of the lens, to one decimal place.

steps.working: 27.5 cm is far below the other three, which lie within 0.6 cm of each other: it is anomalous.
steps.decision: Look for the odd one out before any arithmetic; it can be low as well as high.

options: because it is far from the three that agree
because it is the smallest reading
because it was the third reading taken
whyMenu.explain: A reading is anomalous when it sits far from the others, not because of its size or its place in the list.

steps.working: Leave 27.5 cm out and add the other three: 32.4 + 31.8 + 32.1 = 96.3 cm.
steps.decision: Only the readings that agree go into the mean.

steps.working: Divide by 3: 96.3 ÷ 3 = 32.1 cm.
steps.decision: Divide by how many readings you used, not by how many you took.

twin.stem: A second student records 6.3 cm, 6.1 cm, 8.0 cm and 6.2 cm. Find the focal length of their lens in cm, to one decimal place.

items.stem: Light passes from air into a piece of glass. What happens to its speed?
items.skill: Recalling the change of speed from refraction

options.text: it slows down
options.feedback: Yes, and that is why it changes direction.

options.text: it speeds up
options.feedback: Light is slower in glass than in air, which is why it bends towards the normal on the way in.

options.text: it stays the same
options.feedback: If the speed did not change there would be no refraction at all.

items.stem: A lens has two curved faces, so a ray crossing it is refracted how many times?
items.skill: Counting the boundaries a ray crosses

options.text: twice, once at each face
options.feedback: Yes. That is why the shape of both faces matters.

options.text: once, in the middle
options.feedback: Refraction happens at a boundary between two materials, and a lens has two of them.

options.text: not at all, because glass is transparent
options.feedback: Transparent means the light gets through, not that it carries straight on.

items.stem: Three readings of the same quantity are 6.1 cm, 6.3 cm and 9.8 cm. Which is the anomalous one?

options.text: 9.8 cm
options.feedback: Yes. It sits far outside the group the others form.

options.text: 6.1 cm
options.feedback: 6.1 cm is close to 6.3 cm, so it belongs with the group.

options.text: none of them, because all readings count
options.feedback: A reading well outside the rest is anomalous and is left out of a mean.

items.stem: Which shape of lens brings parallel rays together?

options.text: one that is fat in the middle
options.feedback: Yes: fat in the middle converges.

options.text: one that is thin in the middle
options.feedback: Thin in the middle spreads the rays apart, so that is the diverging lens.

options.text: one with two flat faces
options.feedback: A block with flat parallel faces shifts a ray sideways but does not bring rays together.

options.text: either, depending on which way round it is held
options.feedback: Turning a lens round does not change whether it converges. The shape decides it.

items.stem: Which two points does the focal length of a converging lens run between?

options.text: the optical centre of the lens and the principal focus
options.feedback: Yes, and both names are worth a mark.

options.text: the lens and the screen, whatever the object distance
options.feedback: Lens to screen is only the focal length when the object is distant, so the rays arrive parallel.

options.text: the object and the lens
options.feedback: That is the object distance, which changes as the object moves.

options.text: the two principal focuses on either side
options.feedback: That distance is twice the focal length.

items.stem: The symbol for a lens is a vertical line with arrowheads. Which symbol shows a diverging lens?

options.text: the one with the arrowheads pointing inwards
options.feedback: Yes. Inward arrowheads mean diverging.

options.text: the one with the arrowheads pointing outwards
options.feedback: Outward arrowheads are the converging symbol.

options.text: the one drawn with a dashed line
options.feedback: Dashed lines mean construction lines or a virtual image, not the kind of lens.

options.text: neither: the symbols are the same
options.feedback: The arrowheads are exactly what tells them apart on paper.

items.stem: Why must the object be a long way away when you measure a focal length this way?
items.skill: The reason behind the distant-object method

options.text: so that the light arriving at the lens is almost parallel
options.feedback: Yes, and parallel rays are the ones that meet at the principal focus.

options.text: so that the image on the screen is brighter
options.feedback: A distant object gives a dimmer image, not a brighter one. The reason is that its light arrives parallel.

options.text: so that the image is bigger and easier to measure
options.feedback: A distant object gives a small image. What matters is that its rays arrive parallel.

options.text: so that the lens does not get hot
options.feedback: Heat is not the issue here; the parallel rays are.

items.stem: Four lens-to-screen readings are taken and one is clearly out of line. What should be done with it?

options.text: leave it out and take the mean of the others
options.feedback: Yes. That is exactly the step Booklet B candidates have missed twice.

options.text: include it, because every reading is evidence
options.feedback: An anomalous reading pulls the mean away from the true value, so it is left out.

options.text: use it on its own, because it is the most recent
options.feedback: One reading is never better than the mean of the readings that agree.

options.text: halve it and then include it
options.feedback: There is no reason to halve a reading. It is either kept as it is or left out as an anomaly.

items.stem: Lens P has a focal length of 5 cm and lens Q has a focal length of 20 cm. Which statement is true?
items.skill: Linking focal length to how strongly a lens bends light

options.text: lens P is fatter in the middle and bends light more
options.feedback: Yes. A shorter focal length means the rays are brought together sooner.

options.text: lens Q is fatter in the middle and bends light more
options.feedback: Lens Q takes four times as far to bring rays together, so it bends each one less.

options.text: lens P must be a diverging lens
options.feedback: Both have a focal length and both can be converging; the number only says how strongly each bends light.

options.text: they bend light by the same amount
options.feedback: A focal length of 5 cm and one of 20 cm are very different strengths.

Look at the two lenses in the figure.
Identify the converging lens.

options.text: the lens that is fat in the middle and thin at its edges
options.feedback: Correct. Fat in the middle brings rays together.

options.text: the lens that is thin in the middle and thick at its edges
options.feedback: That one spreads rays apart, so it is the diverging lens.

options.text: both of them, because all lenses bend light inwards
options.feedback: Both bend light, but only one bends it inwards. A lens thin in the middle spreads light out.

scheme.for: the lens that is fat in the middle (convex)

hints: Think about which shape makes the light meet.

parts.stem: State the other name used for a diverging lens.

scheme.for: concave

parts.stem:
In a ray diagram a lens is drawn as a straight vertical line with arrowheads at each end.
State what the arrowheads on the symbol for a converging lens point.

options.text: outwards, away from the axis

options.text: inwards, towards the axis
options.feedback: Inward arrowheads are the diverging symbol.

options.text: along the axis, one each way
options.feedback: The arrowheads sit at the top and bottom of the line, not along the axis.

scheme.for: outwards

hints: The arrowheads copy the shape of the glass.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows a converging lens standing on a horizontal line, with four features marked.
Name each of them.

scheme.for: (i) principal axis
(ii) optical centre
(iii) principal focus
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 P2 Higher: many candidates were unsure where to label the focal point.

scheme.for: (iv) focal length

parts.stem: Describe what a converging lens does to rays that arrive parallel to its principal axis.

accepted: It brings them together at the principal focus.
They are refracted so that they all meet at one point, the principal focus.

parts.stem:
The five steps of the distant-object method for measuring the focal length of a converging lens are listed in the wrong order.
Put them in the order they should be carried out.

expectedOrder: Stand near a window and point the converging lens at a distant object outside.
Hold a white screen on the other side of the lens, in the shadow of the lens.
Move the screen backwards and forwards until the image on it is as sharp as possible.
Measure the distance between the lens centre and the screen with a metre rule.
Repeat the measurement twice more and take the mean of the readings that agree.

parts.workedSolution: 1. Stand near a window and point the converging lens at a distant object outside. 2. Hold a white screen on the other side of the lens, in the shadow of the lens. 3. Repeat the measurement twice more and take the mean of the readings that agree.

parts.workedSolution: Point the converging lens at a distant object, such as a window across the room or a tree outside. options.feedback: A longer focal length means the rays take further to meet, so they have been bent less.

options.text: both the same, because they are both converging lenses

parts.workedSolution: Lens B. Its focal length is 8.4 cm against 14.9 cm for lens A, so it brings parallel rays together in a shorter distance, which means it has bent each ray more.

findTheMistake.stem: A student is working out the focal length of a lens from four readings: 14.8 cm, 15.1 cm, 14.9 cm, 19.4 cm.
studentWorking: The readings are 14.8 cm, 15.1 cm, 14.9 cm, 19.4 cm.

correction: The readings are 14.8 cm, 15.1 cm, 14.9 cm, 19.4 cm, and 19.4 cm is anomalous.
So the focal length of the lens is 14.9 cm.

findTheMistake.stem: A student describes how she measured the focal length of a converging lens.
studentWorking: I pointed the lens at a lamp on my bench.
I moved the screen until the image of the lamp was sharp.
I measured from the middle of the lens to the screen.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: A lamp on the bench is too close: its rays are still spreading when they reach the lens, so they meet further out than F, and the distance she measures is longer than the focal length.
correction: I pointed the lens at a window at the far end of the room.
I moved the screen until the image of the window was sharp.
I measured from the middle of the lens to the screen.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the method's three marks stand: the sharp image and the lens-to-screen distance. The object has to be distant so that its light arrives almost parallel.

prompts.prompt: How do you tell a converging lens from a diverging one?
prompts.answer: Converging is fat in the middle, arrowheads out; diverging is thin in the middle, arrowheads in.

prompts.prompt: What does a converging lens do to rays that arrive parallel to the principal axis?
prompts.answer: It brings them together at one point on the axis, the principal focus.

prompts.prompt: For a converging lens, define the focal length.
prompts.answer: The distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.

prompts.prompt: Where is the principal focus of a diverging lens, and how is it found?
prompts.answer: On the same side as the incoming light, where the backward extensions of the spreading rays cross.

prompts.prompt: Describe the distant-object method in one sentence.
prompts.answer: Focus a distant object on a screen, and measure from the lens to the sharp image.

prompts.prompt: Why does the distant-object method give the focal length rather than some other distance?
prompts.answer: Because light from a distant object arrives almost parallel, and parallel rays meet at the principal focus.

prompts.prompt: Four readings are taken and one is far from the other three. What do you do with it, and why?
prompts.answer: Leave it out of the mean, because it is anomalous and would pull the mean away from the true value.

prompts.prompt: Two converging lenses have focal lengths of 5 cm and 20 cm. Which bends light more, and what does that say about its shape?
prompts.answer: The 5 cm lens bends light more, and it is fatter in the middle.
